builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
summary: EvoTrias replaces monolithic agent-centric evolution loops, where one coding agent both governs the search and proposes candidates, with a three-owner architecture (Structured Governance, Open Proposal, Protected Judgment) that exchanges only typed contracts and can wrap an existing coding agent as a plugin. The cost is additional orchestration complexity: three coordinated components, contract schemas, runtime boundary hooks, and a private evaluator that must be maintained and kept isolated from the proposing agent. What can fail is the judgment boundary in practice, since the Protected Judgment guarantee depends on the evaluator staying private and representative, and the 64% token saving and benchmark gains were measured on the authors' setup and may not transfer to a small team's codebase and budget without workload-specific validation.
rationale: The claimed 64% token-cost reduction and plugin design make it plausible for a constrained team to validate on one representative evolution task, but the architecture's multi-component complexity and unverified third-party implementation maturity argue against immediate production adoption.
technique: Separation-of-powers architecture for agentic program evolution

claims.statement: EvoTrias replaces monolithic agent-centric evolution loops, where one coding agent both governs the search and proposes candidates, with a three-owner architecture (Structured Governance, Open Proposal, Protected Judgment) that exchanges only typed contracts and can wrap an existing coding agent as a plugin. The cost is additional orchestration complexity: three coordinated components, contract schemas, runtime boundary hooks, and a private evaluator that must be maintained and kept isolated from the proposing agent. What can fail is the judgment boundary in practice, since the Protected Judgment guarantee depends on the evaluator staying private and representative, and the 64% token saving and benchmark gains were measured on the authors' setup and may not transfer to a small team's codebase and budget without workload-specific validation.

Separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64% (a roughly 2.8x reduction in token spend) versus agent-centric baselines; the paper also reports state-of-the-art scores on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks.
